title: The Hidden Talent Show
summary: A shy girl who loves to draw finally shares her art at her school's talent show and discovers that her classmates truly admire it.
poll: Everyone should be brave enough to share their talents with others, even if it feels scary.

versions.title: The Hidden Talent Show
versions.text:
Lama loves to draw. She draws cats, cars, and trees. She draws every day. She likes to practice at home. But Lama is shy. She does not like to talk in front of people.

The school has a talent show. Noor is Lama's friend. Noor will sing in the show. Noor says, "Share your art, too!" Lama shakes her head. She feels scared.

Noor does not give up. She says, "Your drawings are special." Lama thinks about it. She goes home. She draws a big picture of the school.

The day of the show comes. Kids sing. Kids dance. Kids tell jokes. Then it is Lama's turn. Her hands shake. She walks onto the stage.

Lama holds up her big picture. The room is quiet. Then kids clap. They clap a lot! A boy says, "That is so good!"

Lama smiles. She is not shy now. Her friends like her art. Lama feels proud.

versions.title: The Hidden Talent Show
versions.text:
Lama loves to draw pictures more than anything else in the world. She draws cats, cars, and trees every day at home. She likes to practice a lot so she can get better. But Lama is very shy, and she does not like to talk in front of other people.

Her school is planning a big talent show this year. Noor, who is Lama's best friend, will sing a song in the show. Noor tells her, "You should share your art too, because it is wonderful!" Lama shakes her head quickly, since the idea makes her feel scared and nervous.

Noor does not give up on her shy friend. She tells Lama, "Your drawings are really special, and everyone should see them." Lama thinks about this for a long while. Finally, she goes home after school and draws a big new picture of her whole school.

On the day of the show, many kids take turns performing. Some kids sing, some dance, and some tell funny jokes on the stage. Then, at last, it is Lama's turn. Her hands shake as she slowly walks onto the bright stage.

Lama holds up her big picture so that everyone in the room can see it clearly. For a moment, the room goes completely quiet. Then, all at once, the kids start to clap loudly and cheer. A boy in the front row shouts, "That picture is amazing!"

Lama smiles brightly at everyone who is watching her. She does not feel shy anymore, not even a little bit. Her classmates truly admire her art, and Lama feels very proud of what she has made.

versions.title: The Hidden Talent Show
versions.text:
Lama loved to draw more than almost anything else in the world. Every day after school, she practiced at home, sketching cats, cars, and trees until each picture looked just right. Despite her talent, Lama was painfully shy. The idea of talking or performing in front of an audience filled her with nervous energy.

One afternoon, her school announced its annual talent show. Noor, Lama's best friend, decided to sing a song in the show and tried to encourage Lama to join her. "You should share your art too," Noor said. "It's wonderful, and people deserve to see it." Lama shook her head quickly. Even the thought of standing in front of the whole school made her stomach twist with nerves.

Still, Noor refused to give up on her shy friend. "Your drawings are special," she insisted, "and everyone at school should get to see them." Lama turned the idea over in her mind for days, slowly gaining a little confidence. Eventually, she decided to go home and draw a brand-new picture, one that showed her entire school from above.

On the day of the show, the auditorium filled with excited students and proud parents. One by one, performers took the stage. Some sang songs, some danced, and others told jokes that made the audience laugh. Finally, it was Lama's turn. Her hands trembled as she walked slowly toward the bright lights of the stage.

Lama lifted her large picture high enough for everyone in the audience to see clearly. For one long moment, the entire room went silent. Then, suddenly, the audience began to clap and cheer loudly. A boy in the front row shouted, "That picture is amazing!"

Lama smiled, feeling a warm rush of pride. Her nervousness had completely disappeared. Her classmates truly admired her unusual talent, and for the first time, Lama felt genuinely confident about who she was.

She tried hard to encourage Lama to join her. "You should share your art too," Noor said warmly. "It's wonderful, and people deserve to see it." Lama shook her head quickly. Even imagining herself standing in front of the whole school made her stomach twist with nerves.

Still, Noor refused to give up on her shy friend. "Your drawings are special," she insisted gently, "and everyone at school should get the chance to see them." Lama turned the idea over in her mind for several days, slowly gaining a little more confidence. Eventually, she decided to go home and draw an entirely new picture, one that showed her whole school seen from high above.

On the day of the show, the school auditorium filled quickly with excited students, curious teachers, and proud parents. One performer after another took the stage. Some sang songs, some danced energetically, and others told jokes that made the audience burst into laughter. Finally, it was Lama's turn. Her hands trembled as she walked slowly toward the bright, glaring lights of the stage.

Lama lifted her large picture high enough for everyone in the audience to see it clearly. For one long, almost unbearable moment, the entire room went completely silent. Then, suddenly, the audience began to clap and cheer loudly, filling the auditorium with noise. A boy in the front row jumped up and shouted, "That picture is amazing!"

Lama smiled, feeling a warm rush of pride spread through her entire body. Her nervousness had completely disappeared, as if it had never existed at all. Her classmates truly admired her unusual talent. For the very first time, Lama felt genuinely confident about who she was.

versions.title: The Hidden Talent Show
versions.text:
Lama loved drawing more than almost anything else in the world, and every day after school she practiced diligently and patiently at home, meticulously sketching cats, cars, and trees until each illustration looked exactly, precisely right. Despite her considerable, undeniable talent, Lama remained hesitant and painfully shy, and the thought of standing in the spotlight in front of an attentive audience filled her with nervous, fluttering apprehension that she could not easily overcome, regardless of how determinedly she attempted to calm herself and steady her trembling hands.

One memorable afternoon, her school administration announced its annual talent show, and considerable anticipation quickly spread throughout the crowded hallways. Noor, Lama's closest and most supportive friend, decided to sing a song in the show and tried persistently to encourage her hesitant friend to participate alongside her, believing wholeheartedly in Lama's unrecognized abilities. "You should share your unique artwork too," Noor said warmly and sincerely, "because it's wonderful, and people genuinely deserve an opportunity to appreciate it." Lama shook her head quickly, since even imagining herself standing in the spotlight in front of the entire school made her stomach twist uncomfortably with apprehension.

Still, Noor absolutely refused to give up on her shy, hesitant friend. "Your drawings are truly extraordinary," she insisted gently and repeatedly, "and everyone at school should genuinely get the opportunity to appreciate them properly." Lama turned the idea over in her mind repeatedly for several days, slowly and steadily accumulating a little more confidence each time she considered it carefully and imagined the possibilities ahead. Eventually, after considerable deliberation, she decided to go home and sketch an entirely new illustration, one that portrayed her whole school as seen from high above the distant, sprawling rooftops.

On the day of the show, the school auditorium filled quickly with excited students, curious teachers, and proud, anticipating parents, all gathering together for this long-awaited occasion. One performer after another confidently took the spotlight, as some sang songs, some danced energetically, and others told jokes that made the audience erupt into uncontrollable laughter. Finally, after what felt like an absolute eternity, it was Lama's turn, and her hands trembled uncontrollably as she walked slowly toward the bright, glaring lights of the stage, determined to overcome her apprehension once and for all.

Lama carefully lifted her large, unique illustration high enough for everyone throughout the audience to see it clearly and completely. For one long, almost unbearable moment, the entire auditorium went completely, eerily silent, and Lama feared that absolutely no one truly understood what she had created. Then, suddenly and unexpectedly, the audience began to clap and cheer enthusiastically, filling the auditorium with overwhelming noise, while a boy sitting in the front row jumped excitedly to his feet and shouted, "That picture is absolutely amazing!"

Lama smiled radiantly, feeling an overwhelming rush of pride and admiration spread throughout her entire body. Her apprehension had completely disappeared, almost as if it had never genuinely existed, and her classmates truly admired her unusual, unique talent wholeheartedly. For the very first time in her life, Lama had overcome her hesitant shyness entirely and felt genuinely, authentically confident about who she was and what she was truly capable of accomplishing.

For the very first time in her life, Lama had overcome her hesitant shyness entirely and felt genuinely, authentically confident about who she was and what she was truly capable of accomplishing.

keyWords.definition: a special skill someone is naturally good at
keyWords.example: Fixing bikes is a talent that Yousef has had since he was little.

keyWords.definition: feeling nervous about talking or being seen by other people
keyWords.example: The new student was shy and sat quietly at the back of the room.

keyWords.definition: a raised platform where people perform in front of an audience
keyWords.example: The band set up their instruments on the stage before the concert.

keyWords.definition: to do something again and again so you get better at it
keyWords.example: My brother practices free throws every afternoon after school.

keyWords.definition: to hit your hands together to show you like something
keyWords.example: The crowd began to clap as soon as the runners crossed the finish line.

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: A boy who learns how to sing very well in music class
A short trip the class takes to an art museum downtown
A shy girl who shares her drawing at a talent show
A teacher who teaches a drawing class after school
questions.why: The story follows Lama as she overcomes being shy and shares her drawing with everyone at the talent show.

wrong.A: The story is about Lama, not a boy who sings.
wrong.B: There is no museum trip in the story.
wrong.D: No teacher gives a drawing class in the story.

questions.stem: What does Lama like to do every day at home?
options: Practice drawing
Sing loudly
Dance around her room
Tell funny jokes
questions.why: The story says Lama draws every day and likes to practice at home.

wrong.B: Singing is what Noor does, not Lama.
wrong.C: The story does not say Lama dances.
wrong.D: The story does not say Lama tells jokes.

questions.stem: Who encourages Lama to join the talent show?
options: Her classroom teacher, who plans school events
Her kind mother, who drives her to school
A boy who sits in her class
Noor, her best friend
questions.why: Noor, who is Lama's best friend, tells her to share her art in the show.

wrong.A: No teacher is mentioned asking Lama to join.
wrong.B: Lama's mother is not in the story.
wrong.C: The boy only speaks after Lama's turn, not before.

questions.stem: In the story, a stage is —
options: a big picture hung on the wall
a place where people perform
a kind of loud, sudden noise
a comfortable chair in the classroom
questions.why: The story says Lama walks onto the stage, the place where kids perform in the show.

wrong.A: A picture is what Lama draws, not a stage.
wrong.C: Clapping is a noise, but a stage is not.
wrong.D: A stage is not a chair.

questions.stem: Why does Lama shake her head when Noor asks her to join the show?
options: She feels shy and scared about performing
She does not like Noor anymore
She does not like to draw pictures
She is too busy at that exact moment to come and help
questions.why: In the story, Lama shakes her head because she feels shy and scared.

wrong.B: Lama and Noor stay good friends in the story.
wrong.C: Lama loves to draw; that is not the reason.
wrong.D: The story does not say Lama is too busy.

questions.stem: What can you tell about Lama after the show?
options: She decides to stop drawing
She feels angry at her classmates
She feels proud and is no longer shy
She wants to sing in the next show
questions.why: After the clapping, Lama smiles, feels proud, and is not shy anymore.

wrong.A: Lama feels proud of her drawing, so she keeps drawing.
wrong.B: Her classmates clap and like her art; she is not angry.
wrong.D: The story does not say Lama wants to sing.

questions.stem: What happens right after the room goes quiet?
options: Lama leaves the stage
The teacher turns off the lights
Everyone starts to talk at once
The kids start to clap loudly
questions.why: In the story, the room is quiet for a moment, and then the kids clap.

wrong.A: Lama stays on stage holding up her picture.
wrong.B: The story does not mention the lights.
wrong.C: The kids clap; the story does not say they all talk.

questions.stem: Why does the author tell us that Lama's hands shake as she walks onto the stage?
options: To show that the classroom felt cold that day
To show how nervous she feels before she performs
To explain that Lama suddenly felt sick
To show that she feels angry at her friend Noor
questions.why: Shaking hands show how nervous and scared Lama feels right before she shows her picture.

wrong.A: The story never says the room was cold.
wrong.C: The story does not say Lama is sick.
wrong.D: Lama is not angry at Noor; Noor helped her.

LOW.prompt: Would you be brave enough to share something you made with your whole class, even if it felt scary? Explain, using at least two facts from the story.
checklist: I clearly said what I think.
I used at least two facts from the story.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: I think I would be brave enough to share something I made. I remember that Lama was very shy at first, but her friend Noor would not give up on encouraging her. In the end, the kids clapped loudly and told Lama that her picture was amazing. That shows that being brave can lead to something good.

keyWords.definition: a group of people who gather to watch or listen to a performance
keyWords.example: The audience grew quiet as the magician began his trick.

keyWords.definition: feeling worried or uneasy about something that is about to happen
keyWords.example: I always feel nervous before the first day of a new school year.

keyWords.definition: to give someone confidence or support to try something
keyWords.example: Our coach likes to encourage us even after we lose a game.

keyWords.definition: a feeling of trust in your own ability to do something well
keyWords.example: Winning the spelling bee gave Huda a lot of confidence.

keyWords.definition: to do something, such as sing or act, in front of an audience
keyWords.example: The dancers will perform in the school gym on Friday night.

questions.stem: What is the best summary of this story?
options: A shy, talented artist slowly builds the courage to share her drawing with an audience, who end up admiring it
A group of close friends spends weeks planning a surprise class trip to an art museum, and the trip is a big success
A nervous boy practices singing for weeks before performing in front of a large audience
A school teacher spends the whole year organizing a big talent show for every single student
questions.why: The story follows Lama as she gains confidence to perform, and her audience ends up admiring her drawing.

wrong.B: There is no museum trip in the story.
wrong.C: Noor, not Lama, is the one who sings.
wrong.D: The story focuses on Lama, not on a teacher organizing the show.

questions.stem: What does Noor do in the talent show?
options: She tells jokes on stage
She dances with her classmates
She sings a song
She paints a picture during the show
questions.why: The story says Noor decided to sing a song in the show.

wrong.A: Other performers tell jokes, not Noor.
wrong.B: The story does not say Noor dances.
wrong.D: Lama, not Noor, makes the picture, and she does it at home, not during the show.

questions.stem: What does Lama's new picture show?
options: A map of her neighborhood streets
Her whole school seen from high above
A portrait of her best friend Noor
The inside of the school auditorium
questions.why: In the story, Lama draws a new picture that shows her whole school seen from high above.

wrong.A: The picture shows the school, not neighborhood streets.
wrong.C: The picture is of the school, not of Noor.
wrong.D: The picture shows the school from above, not the inside of the auditorium.

questions.stem: In the story, to encourage someone means to —
options: force them to do something they hate
ignore what they want to do
laugh at their ideas and ability
give them confidence to try something
questions.why: Noor encourages Lama by telling her that her drawings are special, giving her confidence to try performing.

wrong.A: Noor never forces Lama; she gently asks.
wrong.B: Noor pays close attention to Lama, not ignores her.
wrong.C: Noor never laughs at Lama's drawings.

questions.stem: Why does Lama's confidence slowly grow in the days before the show?
options: Because her teacher gives her a trophy
Because she stops practicing her drawing
Because of Noor's encouraging words
Because the show is suddenly canceled
questions.why: The story says Lama turns the idea over in her mind for days, slowly gaining confidence after hearing Noor's words.

wrong.A: No teacher gives Lama a trophy in the story.
wrong.B: Lama keeps drawing a brand-new picture; she does not stop.
wrong.D: The show is not canceled; it happens as planned.

questions.stem: Why does the audience go silent right after Lama lifts her picture?
options: They are surprised by her picture
They cannot see the picture
They are upset that she interrupted the show
They are waiting for the next performer to start
questions.why: The silence happens the moment everyone sees the big picture clearly, right before they start clapping and cheering.

wrong.B: Lama lifts the picture so everyone can see it clearly.
wrong.C: It is Lama's planned turn, not an interruption.
wrong.D: The silence is about Lama's picture, not about waiting for someone else.

questions.stem: What mainly causes Lama's nervousness to disappear by the end of the show?
options: Noor sings a second song for her
The teacher tells her to stop worrying
She remembers to breathe slowly
The audience cheers for her picture
questions.why: The story says once the audience begins clapping and cheering, Lama's nervousness completely disappears.

wrong.A: Noor sings only once, earlier in the show.
wrong.B: No teacher speaks to Lama in the story.
wrong.C: The story does not mention breathing slowly.

questions.stem: How does the author mainly organize the events in this story?
options: By comparing Lama's drawings with Noor's singing
By telling events in the order they happened
By listing reasons why talent shows are useful
By explaining step-by-step how to draw a school building
questions.why: The story moves in time order: Lama practices, Noor encourages her, she draws a new picture, and then she performs.

wrong.A: The story does not compare their talents side by side.
wrong.C: The story never lists reasons talent shows are useful.
wrong.D: The story never explains drawing steps.

MID.prompt: Explain how Noor helps Lama become confident enough to perform. Use at least two details from the story.
checklist: I used at least two details from the story.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: Noor helps Lama become confident in a few ways. First, Noor refuses to give up on her shy friend, even after Lama shakes her head. Then Noor tells Lama that her drawings are special and that everyone should see them. Hearing this again and again helps Lama slowly gain the confidence to draw a brand-new picture and finally share it at the show.

keyWords.definition: unsure or unwilling to do something because of fear or doubt
keyWords.example: He was hesitant to raise his hand, even though he knew the answer.

keyWords.definition: a strong feeling of respect and liking for someone or something impressive
keyWords.example: The crowd watched the gymnast's routine with real admiration.

keyWords.definition: the strong light aimed at a performer on stage, or the attention of being watched
keyWords.example: The violinist stood alone in the spotlight before the music began.

keyWords.definition: to successfully deal with or defeat a difficulty or fear
keyWords.example: It took months of lessons for Rana to overcome her fear of swimming.

keyWords.definition: being the only one of its kind; unlike anything else
keyWords.example: Every snowflake that falls has a unique shape.

questions.stem: Which sentence best captures the central idea of this story?
options: A teacher designs an elaborate talent show to raise school spirit
A group of students compete fiercely to win first place at a competition
An artist decides never to draw again after a disappointing performance
A shy artist overcomes her fear and earns her classmates' admiration
questions.why: The story centers on Lama overcoming her hesitation to perform and finding that her classmates admire her unique drawing.

wrong.A: The teacher only announces the show; the story focuses on Lama.
wrong.B: The story is not about a competition for first place.
wrong.C: Lama's performance goes well, and she does not give up on drawing.

questions.stem: What does Lama's final illustration specifically portray?
options: Her school seen from high above
A portrait of Noor singing on stage
A map of the surrounding neighborhood
The inside of the crowded auditorium
questions.why: In the story, Lama's new illustration portrays her whole school as seen from high above the rooftops.

wrong.B: Lama draws her school, not a portrait of Noor.
wrong.C: The illustration is of the school building, not the neighborhood.
wrong.D: The illustration shows the school from outside, not the auditorium's interior.

questions.stem: What does Noor repeatedly tell Lama in order to persuade her to participate?
options: That the show will be canceled unless more students join
That drawing is easier than singing
That her drawings are extraordinary
That the audience will not actually be watching closely
questions.why: Noor insists several times that Lama's drawings are truly special or extraordinary and deserve to be seen.

wrong.A: Noor never says the show depends on more students.
wrong.B: Noor never compares drawing with singing.
wrong.D: Noor never suggests the audience will not pay attention.

questions.stem: In the story, the word hesitant most nearly means —
options: excited and eager to begin immediately
unsure and reluctant from fear
angry about an unfair decision
confident and self-assured
questions.why: Lama's hesitation comes from her shyness and fear of the spotlight, which is why Noor keeps encouraging her.

wrong.A: Lama is reluctant, not eager, to perform at first.
wrong.C: Lama is not angry at anyone in the story.
wrong.D: Lama lacks confidence at first, which is why she hesitates.

questions.stem: Why does the idea of standing in the spotlight provoke such intense apprehension in Lama specifically?
options: Because she is naturally very shy
Because she has never practiced her drawing before
Because she dislikes her classmates personally
Because she does not understand what a talent show is
questions.why: Since Lama is described as painfully shy, standing in front of an audience naturally fills her with apprehension about being watched.

wrong.B: Lama practices diligently at home; lack of practice is not the issue.
wrong.C: Nothing suggests Lama dislikes her classmates.
wrong.D: Lama understands the show well enough to eventually join it.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about Noor's role in Lama's eventual change by the end of the story?
options: Noor discouraged Lama from joining the show at first
Noor performed Lama's part for her on stage
Noor had no real effect on Lama's decision
Noor's encouragement helped Lama overcome her fear
questions.why: Noor repeatedly encourages Lama despite her refusals, and this persistence is what finally helps Lama gain the courage to perform.

wrong.A: Noor encourages Lama from the very beginning, not discourages her.
wrong.B: Lama performs her own part; Noor only sings her own song.
wrong.C: Noor's words clearly change Lama's mind over several days.

questions.stem: Which lists these events in the order they actually happened?
options: Lama performs, the school announces the show, Noor encourages Lama, and the audience applauds
The audience applauds, Lama draws her picture, the school announces the show, and Noor encourages her
The school announces the show, Noor encourages Lama, Lama draws her picture, Lama performs
Noor encourages Lama, Lama performs, the school announces the show, and Lama draws her picture
questions.why: The school first announces the show, then Noor encourages Lama, then Lama draws her new illustration, and finally she performs.

wrong.A: The announcement and encouragement happen before Lama performs.
wrong.B: The applause happens after Lama performs, not before.
wrong.D: The school announces the show before Noor ever encourages Lama.

questions.stem: Why does the author emphasize the audience's total silence immediately before they erupt into applause?
options: To suggest that the audience actually disliked the picture
To build suspense about the audience's reaction
To show that the auditorium's lights had suddenly failed
To explain why the show ended early that day
questions.why: The brief, unbearable silence makes readers wonder how the audience will react, right before the cheering reveals genuine admiration.

wrong.A: The audience ends up cheering enthusiastically, showing they liked it.
wrong.C: The story never mentions the lights failing.
wrong.D: The show continues normally; it does not end early.

HIGH.prompt: The poll says everyone should be brave enough to share their talents, even if it feels scary. Do you agree or disagree? Support your argument with evidence from the story about Lama's hesitation, Noor's encouragement, and the audience's reaction.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the poll statement.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the story.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that everyone should be brave enough to share their talents, even when it feels frightening. Lama was hesitant and painfully shy, yet with Noor's persistent encouragement, she managed to overcome her fear of the spotlight. When she finally revealed her unique illustration, the audience responded with genuine admiration instead of the judgment she had feared. Someone might argue that performing is simply too stressful for a shy person, but Lama's experience shows that facing that fear, with support from a good friend, can lead to a result far better than she expected.

LOW.stem: What does Noor do in the talent show?
options: She tells jokes
She draws a cat
She sings
She dances on the stage
LOW.why: In the story, Noor will sing in the show.

wrong.A: Other kids tell jokes, but Noor sings.
wrong.B: Lama is the one who draws, not Noor.
wrong.D: Other kids dance, but Noor sings.

LOW.stem: What does Lama draw for the show?
options: A big picture of the school
A small picture of a cat
A picture of her friend Noor
A new picture of a tall tree
LOW.why: The text says she goes home and draws a big picture of the school.

wrong.B: She draws cats at other times, but not for the show.
wrong.C: The text does not say she draws Noor.
wrong.D: Trees are in her usual drawings, not this picture.

LOW.stem: In the story, what does "proud" mean?
options: Afraid of something very big
Tired from a long, hard school day
Sad about a mistake
Happy about something you did well
LOW.why: Lama smiles when kids clap for her art, so proud means happy about what she did.

wrong.A: Lama is not afraid at the end.
wrong.B: The story does not say she is tired.
wrong.C: She smiles, so she is not sad.

LOW.stem: Why does Lama go home and draw a big picture?
options: Her teacher gives her homework
Noor says her drawings are special
Her mother tells her to draw
She wants to win a prize
LOW.why: In the story, Noor tells Lama her drawings are special, and then Lama thinks about it and goes home.

wrong.A: The text does not say it is homework.
wrong.C: Her mother is not in the story.
wrong.D: No prize is mentioned in the story.

MID.stem: What did Lama sketch when she practiced at home?
options: Cats, cars, and trees
Birds, boats, and houses
Flowers, books, and chairs
Friends, teachers, and parents
MID.why: The text says she sketched cats, cars, and trees every day after school.

wrong.B: Birds, boats, and houses are not named.
wrong.C: Flowers, books, and chairs are not named.
wrong.D: People are not listed in her practice drawings.

MID.stem: In the story, what does the word "admired" mean?
options: Forgot about
Laughed at
Was afraid of
Liked and respected
MID.why: The classmates clapped and cheered, so they admired her talent by respecting it.

wrong.A: They paid attention to her picture.
wrong.B: They cheered, so they did not laugh at her.
wrong.C: The text does not say they were afraid.

MID.stem: Why does Noor say that people deserve to see Lama's art?
options: She wants Lama to win the whole talent show
She believes Lama's art is good enough to share
She wants to sing alone on stage
She thinks Lama should stop being shy
MID.why: Noor says the art is wonderful, so she believes it is good enough for others to see.

wrong.A: Noor never talks about winning.
wrong.C: Noor wants Lama to join, not to leave her alone.
wrong.D: Noor does not say Lama must stop being shy; she praises her art.

MID.stem: Why does the author describe the singers, dancers, and joke tellers?
options: To show that Noor is the best performer
To explain how to plan a talent show
To show that the show had many kinds of talents
To tell the reader that parents were angry
MID.why: The author lists the singing, dancing, and jokes to show the show had many kinds of talents before Lama's turn.

wrong.A: Noor is only one of the singers.
wrong.B: The article is not a how-to guide.
wrong.D: The parents were proud, not angry.

HIGH.stem: Who filled the auditorium on the day of the show?
options: Only the students in Lama's class
Students, teachers, and parents
Teachers and the principal only
Local artists and visitors
HIGH.why: The text says the auditorium filled with excited students, curious teachers, and proud parents.

wrong.A: The audience included more than one class.
wrong.C: Students and parents were there too.
wrong.D: Local artists and visitors are not mentioned.

HIGH.stem: In the article, the word "diligently" most nearly means —
options: with careful and steady effort
with very great speed and energy
in a lazy way
with a loud voice
HIGH.why: Lama practiced every day until each picture looked exactly right, which shows steady effort.

wrong.B: Practicing every day until it is right is about effort, not speed.
wrong.C: Lazy does not fit someone who practiced every day.
wrong.D: Voice has nothing to do with drawing.

HIGH.stem: What led Lama to decide to draw a new picture?
options: The teachers asked her to draw it for the show
She wanted to beat Noor in the show
Noor kept encouraging her, and her confidence slowly grew
She had nothing else to do at home after school each day
HIGH.why: Noor refused to give up, and Lama slowly gained confidence over several days before she sketched the new picture.

wrong.A: The teachers are not said to ask her.
wrong.B: Noor is a friend and is singing, so they are not competing.
wrong.D: The text shows a choice made after thinking, not boredom.

HIGH.stem: Why does the author write that Lama's nervousness disappeared as if it had never existed?
options: To show Lama forgot her picture
To suggest the show was not important
To explain that Noor was never nervous
To show how complete the change in Lama was
HIGH.why: The phrase shows her nervousness was gone completely after the audience cheered.

wrong.A: Lama remembers her picture; she is proud of it.
wrong.B: The show is important to Lama.
wrong.C: The phrase is about Lama, not Noor.
